S_how.S1: I judged how cute each animal and photo would look to a typical adult, by species type (young and furry animals, cats and dogs above average; fish, reptiles, amphibians and large horned or tusked animals below), then pulled every estimate toward the overall level of the 24 example pictures (mean about 5.6, mostly 4 to 7). Those examples follow intuitive cuteness only loosely, so these numbers are rough estimates, not known values.
S_how.S2: I looked at all six sheets and used the 24 reference ratings to set the scale. Those ratings are fairly compressed, with most around 4 to 7, and they vary a lot within a single animal type: the two eagles got 4.0 and 6.85, and the cats ranged from 3.8 to 6.3. So I placed each numbered picture by its animal type (dogs, kittens/cats and young animals high; fish, amphibians, reptiles and horned ungulates low), adjusted for how appealing the pose and framing looked, and pulled my guesses toward the overall average of about 5.5.
S_how.S3: The 24 reference pictures showed only a weak, partly counter-intuitive link between how kawaii an animal looks and its score (for example the fox got 7.63, the frog 6.92 and the eagles about 6.8–6.9, while a cat got 3.80 and the Doberman 2.97), so I kept every estimate close to the reference average of about 5.6 and only nudged each one slightly up or down by how kawaii the animal and photo usually look; these are low-confidence guesses, and I don't expect them to rank individual pictures reliably.
S_how.S4: I looked at each picture and estimated the crowd's rating by comparing it with the 24 anchor pictures and their given ratings: mammals with soft faces, young animals and pets near the top, reptiles, fish and amphibians near the bottom, and everything kept within the compressed, noisy range the anchors show (roughly 3 to 7.6).
S_how.S5: I estimated how cute each picture looks and pulled every estimate strongly toward the reference average of about 5.6. In the T1–T24 reference set, the ratings barely track how cute the pictures look: a bunny got 4.30, a black-and-white cat 3.80 and a Doberman 2.97, while a poison frog got 6.92, an eagle 6.85 and a fox 7.63. So these are low-confidence guesses that stay close to the average, not readings from data.
S_how.S6: I estimated each picture from its animal type and how it looks (baby-like features, pets, mammals versus fish and reptiles), then pulled the numbers toward the T1-T24 average of about 5.6 because those reference ratings track ordinary ideas of cuteness only loosely (for example, the eagle got 6.85 and the black-and-white cat 3.80).

how.A1: I looked at each picture once and scored it by how strongly it brought out the kawaii features I respond to: baby-like or round, soft-looking bodies, big eyes, fluffy texture, playful or sleepy poses and endearing expressions; scaly, armored, horned or predatory-looking animals scored low.
how.A2: I looked at each picture and scored it by gut feeling. The things that pushed a score up were baby-like or soft round features, fluffy fur, big eyes, and charming moments like a cat with its tongue out, a sleeping kitten or a puppy playing with a ball. The things that pulled it down were reptiles, fish, horns, tusks and harsh or predatory looks.
how.A3: I looked at each picture and rated it on my own sense of kawaii, scoring higher for babies and young animals, round soft or fluffy bodies, big eyes, and playful or sleepy poses, and lower for scaly, slimy or rough-skinned animals and stern or predatory looks.
how.A4: I looked at all four sheets and gave each picture a 1–9 rating on my own gut sense of kawaii; young animals, round soft shapes, big eyes and playful or endearing poses scored high, and reptiles, fish and hard or tough-looking animals scored low.
how.A5: I looked at each picture myself and scored how strongly it reads as cute: soft, fluffy, round shapes, big eyes, a young or small-looking animal and endearing poses or expressions (a sleeping kitten, a tongue out, a fawn) scored high, while scaly, armoured, horned or menacing animals, and neutral documentary shots, scored low.
how.A6: I looked at all four sheets and rated each picture on my own gut sense of kawaii, scoring higher for soft, round, baby-like features, big eyes and endearing poses or expressions (like the puppy with the ball, the fawn, the sleeping cat, the baby orangutan and the owl) and lower for scaly, armored, horned or fierce-looking animals (like the fish, the crocodile, the rhino and the toad).
how.D1: I looked at each picture once and estimated the typical kawaii rating that Japanese adults in a crowdsourced sample would give it. I based this on the type of animal (pets and young or furry mammals rate high; reptiles, amphibians and fish rate low), on the pose and expression, and on how such samples tend to cluster toward the middle of the scale. These are guesses, not measured data.
how.D2: I looked at each picture and guessed the group's ratings from the kind of animal (pets, young animals and small furry mammals higher; fish, amphibians, reptiles and large or horned animals lower), the pose and expression, and how Japanese adults tend to use a 1-9 rating scale (pulled toward the middle), so these are estimates and not recalled data.
how.D3: I looked at each picture on the four sheets and estimated the panel's ratings from the animal type (cats, dogs and young animals high; reptiles, amphibians and fish low) and from the pose and expression, using what I know about how Japanese adults tend to judge kawaii.
how.D4: I looked at each of the four sheets and estimated by judgement how Japanese adults would probably rate each picture, using the animal type (cats, dogs and young animals rate high, reptiles, amphibians and fish rate low) and the photo's features (face shown, pose, how baby-like it looks), so these are guesses and not real data.
how.D5: I looked at the four sheets and estimated each picture's crowd rating from the kind of animal (cats, young animals and puppies high; fish, reptiles, amphibians and large rough-skinned mammals low) and from the pose and expression, then pulled the means toward the middle of the scale because averages over about 57 raters are compressed.
how.D6: I looked at the four picture sheets and estimated each picture's median and mean from what I'd expect of Japanese adults' kawaii ratings. I placed pictures by animal type (cats and dogs high, mammals in the middle, fish, crocodile and amphibians low), then adjusted for pose, facial expression and baby-like features. These numbers are my estimates, not the study's actual data.
how.B1: I estimated each picture by comparing it with the 24 calibration pictures. Cats scored about 6.8, dogs about 6 to 6.8, the rabbit 7.6, raptors about 4 and reptiles or amphibians about 3 to 4. I then shifted each estimate for the kind of animal, whether it looked young, its pose and its expression, and how attractive the photo was.
how.B2: I looked at all 72 pictures and placed each of the 48 by comparing it with the 24 rated examples, mainly by kind of animal (cats and dogs high, birds of prey, primates and big hoofed animals in the middle to low, amphibians, fish and reptiles lowest), then nudged it for things like being a baby, the pose and how the photo was taken.
how.B3: I matched each picture to the most similar reference pictures (T1-T24) by species, pose and appeal, set my estimates against their known ratings, and adjusted for features such as baby animals, fur and big eyes versus reptiles, fish and amphibians.
how.B4: I looked at each picture and estimated the ratings by comparing it with the 24 rated T pictures (cats about 6.8 to 6.9, the rabbit 7.6, the wallaby 6.85, the eagles 4.0 to 4.6, the chameleon 3.8, the poison frog 2.97), adjusting for the kind of animal, whether it looked young, its pose and the photo, so these are judgment-based guesses and not measured data.
how.B5: I looked at the 24 reference pictures to see how the scores ran by kind of animal (cats and dogs about 6 to 7.6, wallaby and fox high, eagles, pig and monkey around 4 to 4.5, frog and chameleon about 3 to 4), then estimated each numbered picture by comparing its animal type, whether it looked young, its pose and expression, and the photo framing with those references.
how.B6: I matched each picture to the 24 rated reference pictures by animal type, how it looks and how it is posed (cats and dogs about 6.5-7.3, reptiles, amphibians and fish about 2.5-3, large wild animals and primates about 4-5), then adjusted each one for things like a young animal, a playful pose or a close-up face.
